Japanese parrotfish (Calotomus japonicus) exhibits a distinct pattern of reproductive allocation that reflects its life history strategy within the family Scaridae. Field surveys in the coastal waters of southern Japan documented a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 4% [GSI = 4%] for reproductively active individuals sampled at a seawater temperature of 20.5 °C [T = 20.5 °C]. The measurement was obtained through standard dissections of mature specimens during the peak of the summer spawning aggregation, with gonads excised and weighed to the nearest 0.001 g. Such values are consistent with those reported for other temperate parrotfishes that exhibit prolonged spawning seasons, wherein energetic resources are allocated gradually toward gamete production over several months.

Recorded growth trajectories for Japanese parrotfish indicate that individuals ultimately reach a total length of 39 cm [Li = 39 cm], which represents the asymptotic size documented from extensive mark-recapture studies across their range. This ultimate length is attained after a prolonged growth phase that slows considerably following the onset of reproductive maturity. Corresponding body mass at this maximum size has been estimated using length-weight relationships derived from over three hundred specimens collected during fishery-independent surveys, yielding an ultimate wet weight of 1150 grams [Wwi = 1150 grams]. This substantial body size places Calotomus japonicus among the larger members of its genus, and the relationship between length and mass follows a power function typical of fusiform reef fishes. The growth curve data further reveal that most individuals approach this asymptotic size by approximately their sixth or seventh year, after which somatic growth becomes negligible and energetic resources are instead channeled primarily toward reproductive functions and maintenance.

The onset of reproductive development in Japanese parrotfish occurs when individuals attain a total length of 20 cm [Lp = 20 cm], a threshold that corresponds to the onset of gonadal maturation based on histological examination of specimens collected across multiple seasons. At this length at puberty, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is 157.4 grams [Wwp = 157.4 grams], a value derived from the same allometric length-weight equation that describes the broader population. This represents roughly thirteen percent of the ultimate wet weight, indicating that sexual maturation occurs relatively early in the species' ontogeny compared to some larger-bodied scarids. The early onset of reproductive capability may confer a selective advantage in temperate environments where growing seasons are shorter and the window for successful spawning is more constrained. Histological analyses of gonadal tissue from individuals at or near this size confirm the presence of developing oocytes in females and active spermatogenic crypts in males.

At the earliest stage of life, the newly hatched yolk-sac larva of Japanese parrotfish emerges from an egg measuring approximately 0.66 mm in diameter, which corresponds to a computed wet weight at birth of 0.00015 grams [Wwb = 0.00015 grams]. This remarkably small initial mass—calculated from the spherical egg volume assuming a density close to that of seawater—reflects the typical pattern for marine teleosts that produce numerous small pelagic eggs. The pelagic egg itself is transparent and buoyant, drifting with ocean currents during the incubation period that lasts roughly 24 to 30 hours at 20.5 °C [T = 20.5 °C]. Following eclosion, the yolk-sac larva remains entirely dependent on its endogenous yolk reserves for the first few days before the onset of first exogenous feeding. The lecithotrophic phase is a critical window during which the larva must complete yolk-sac resorption and develop functional feeding structures before encountering the point of no return.

Estimates of maximum longevity for Calotomus japonicus have been derived from annual growth increment counts on sagittal otoliths, indicating a lifespan of approximately 2,920 days [am = approximately 2,920 days] under natural conditions at an average water temperature of 20.5 °C [T = 20.5 °C]. This places it within the moderate range for temperate parrotfishes, where lifespan often correlates inversely with metabolic rate and directly with body size. The otolith-based age estimates were validated through marginal increment analysis and corroborated by recaptures of tagged individuals over a decade-long monitoring program. Such a lifespan allows for multiple reproductive seasons, with individuals typically spawning once per year during the summer months.
